newsitem.title: USA: California governor proposes $1 bln tax cut.
newsitem.headline: California governor proposes $1 bln tax cut.

text.p: California Gov. Pete Wilson and Republican state legislative leaders on Wednesday proposed a $1 billion middle-class tax cut.

"With this state's economy surpassing all expectations, the time has come both to provide tax relief for those Californians who surrender too much of their paychecks to Sacramento and to provide assurance that state government will not automatically, gluttonously spend all the growing bonanza in tax revenues, simply because the money is there," Wilson, a Republican, said in a statement.
Wilson's proposal would increase the current tax-bracket ceiling by 10 percent beginning with the 1999 tax year.
He said his proposal would allow a single taxpayer earning $40,000 a year to receive a $166 tax cut, and a couple earning a combined $80,000 to get a $332 tax break.
"This is a sensible way to give tax relief to working Californians," Wilson said.
Wilson also proposed a one percent increase in state employee salaries, and offered to scale back his plan for a bank and corporation tax cut to five percent from 10 percent.
Senate President Pro Tem Bill Lockyer, a Democrat, said he opposed the governor's $1 billion tax cut plan because it would cut too deeply into education funding.
Lockyer said the tax cut plan could complicate ongoing budget negotiations. "It probably will be a little more difficult to reach a conclusion," he said.

Welfare reform and education funding have been the major stumbling block for lawmakers negotiating the state's spending plan for the 1997-1998 fiscal year, which began July 1. The state's Constitutional budget deadline was June 15.
